The Mexican climbing salamander (Bolitoglossa mexicana) is a lungless plethodontid that develops directly from terrestrial eggs, bypassing the free-swimming larval stage common among many amphibians. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the period of embryonic development culminates in hatching after approximately 63 days [ab = approximately 63 days], yielding fully formed, miniature versions of the adults. These neonates emerge from the gel capsule weighing a mere 0.05 grams [Wwb = 0.05 grams], a value reflecting the species' investment in a relatively small number of yolk-rich eggs. The snout-vent length at this hatching event averages just 0.95 centimeters [Lb = 0.95 centimeters], highlighting the diminutive starting point from which growth proceeds. Subsequent development follows a gradual trajectory typical of tropical plethodontids, with juveniles feeding on small arthropods and growing steadily under the humid forest conditions they inhabit. This lengthy incubation period compared to other Neotropical salamanders likely correlates with the substantial yolk reserves that sustain the embryo until emergence.

Sexual maturation in Bolitoglossa mexicana exhibits marked dimorphism, with females attaining puberty at a considerably larger body size than males. Females reach reproductive maturity once their snout-vent length approaches 7.8 centimeters [Lp = 7.8 centimeters], a size that may not be achieved until well into their second decade of life given the species' slow growth rate. By contrast, males commence gametogenesis at a substantially smaller body size, achieving puberty when their SVL measures approximately 5 centimeters [Lp = approximately 5 centimeters]. This divergence in maturation thresholds is consistent with the greater energetic demands of egg production and the need for females to accommodate a developing clutch within their body cavity. The size differential also shapes the species' reproductive ecology, as larger females are able to produce more eggs per clutch and likely enjoy higher reproductive success. Population surveys in the lowland forests of Veracruz and Chiapas have documented that this sexual size dimorphism persists throughout adulthood.

The ultimate body size attained by adult Mexican climbing salamanders provides insight into the species' position within the plethodontid life-history continuum. Field measurements indicate that the maximum snout-vent length reaches approximately 10 centimeters [Li = approximately 10 centimeters], derived from a total length of about 20 centimeters given the typical tail-to-body proportion of this genus. This places Bolitoglossa mexicana among the medium-to-large members of its species-rich genus, which spans a wide range of adult sizes across Central America. In terms of mass, the ultimate wet weight recorded for fully grown individuals is 78.2 grams [Wwi = 78.2 grams], a robust figure reflecting the salamander's heavy-bodied build and relatively short, muscular limbs adapted for arboreal climbing. This considerable adult mass represents a substantial increase from the 0.05 gram neonates, involving a more than 1,500-fold gain over the course of the growth period. Such a dramatic ontogenetic transformation underscores the critical importance of consistent prey availability in the species' forest-floor and low-vegetation microhabitats.

The reproductive output of Bolitoglossa mexicana follows a pattern typical of tropical plethodontids, characterized by relatively small clutches but repeated breeding events per year. At a stable temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females produce between 26 and 40 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 26 and 40 eggs per clutch], depositing them in gelatinous masses within moist crevices or beneath rotting logs. This moderate fecundity is offset by the capacity to produce approximately two clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately two clutches each year], allowing for substantial annual reproductive effort despite the prolonged developmental period of each clutch. The incubation period of roughly two months each time means that reproductively active females spend a considerable portion of the year either carrying eggs or guarding a freshly deposited nest. Brood attendance by the female is common in this species, as she remains coiled around the egg mass to prevent desiccation and fungal infection, behaviors that enhance offspring survival but impose energetic costs that may limit clutch frequency in nutritionally stressed individuals.

Longevity records for Bolitoglossa mexicana indicate an exceptionally extended lifespan for an amphibian of its size, reflecting the slow pace of life characteristic of many tropical plethodontids. Under consistent thermal conditions of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum documented lifespan reaches approximately 35 years [am = approximately 35 years], a duration more typical of small mammals or birds than of most neotropical frogs and toads. This remarkable longevity is supported by the species' low metabolic rate, its reliance on cutaneous respiration in a consistently humid environment, and its ability to avoid many of the desiccation risks that shorten the lives of other amphibians. The long lifespan also permits multiple reproductive seasons, which is advantageous given the extended period required to reach sexual maturity and the relatively low annual fecundity. Individuals that survive to old age may thus contribute offspring over many consecutive years, buffering the population against occasional years of poor recruitment. This life-history strategy aligns well with the stable, aseasonal environments of the tropical lowland forests Bolitoglossa mexicana inhabits.
